implementation_notes: std::sync::mpsc ships the queue pair: channel() is the unbounded variant whose send never blocks, sync_channel(n) is bounded and makes send park once the buffer is full, recv() blocks the consumer and try_recv() polls without blocking; cloning the Sender gives fan-in while the Receiver stays single-consumer. What replaces the classic structure is the channel plus ownership - events are moved into the queue, so there is no shared mutable queue to lock and the compiler enforces the hand-off. An explicit VecDeque is still justified for a lock-step tick drain, and crossbeam-channel when multiple consumers are required.
pitfalls: mpsc allows exactly one Receiver: a work-sharing design needs a Mutex<Receiver>, a different queue such as crossbeam-channel, or one channel per worker.

send returns Err(SendError) once the receiver is dropped - unwrapping what looks impossible turns an ordinary shutdown into a panic, and try_send on a full sync_channel yields TrySendError::Full instead of blocking.
The unbounded channel hides back-pressure and allocates per message, so a fast producer grows memory without limit.
